entities.name: Theodore of Mopsuestia
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Theodore of Mopsuestia, consecrated Bishop of Mopsuestia in Cilicia in 392 CE, stands as a towering intellect of the early Christian Church, widely regarded as the most articulate exponent of the Antiochene School of theology. Born in Antioch around 350 CE, he received a classical education and theological training under the renowned Diodore of Tarsus, alongside his close friend John Chrysostom. Theodore's profound exegetical work, emphasizing a literal and historical interpretation of scripture over the prevalent Alexandrian allegorical method, laid the intellectual groundwork for a distinct Christological tradition that would profoundly shape the theological landscape of the 5th and 6th centuries across the Roman and Persian Empires.

His core contributions centered on Christology, where he meticulously defended the distinctness of Christ's divine and human natures, united in a single 'prosopon' (person or external manifestation) but without confusion or mixture. Theodore vigorously opposed Apollinarianism, which denied a complete human soul to Christ, and his nuanced arguments aimed to preserve both Christ's full humanity and full divinity. He produced extensive commentaries on nearly all books of the Bible, though many are lost, and his sermons and treatises articulated a systematic theological vision that prioritized human free will and the integrity of Christ's two natures. His work was foundational for understanding the Incarnation within the Antiochene intellectual tradition, influencing generations of theologians.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Theodore of Mopsuestia's detailed Christological and exegetical work profoundly shaped the Antiochene theological tradition, directly influencing key figures like Nestorius and becoming foundational for the Church of the East, thus driving centuries of theological debate and contributing to major Christian schisms.
